title: Frequency‑domain enhanced bi‑directional recurrent quantum network for stock price trend prediction
abstract_summary: The paper proposes FDBRQ, a multistep stock price trend prediction model that combines a frequency-domain embedding module (FDEM), an external feature attention enhancement (EFAE) using exogenous factors, and a bi-directional recurrent quantum neural network built from quantum circuit units. Designed to handle non-stationary, long-memory and noisy financial time series, the method outputs multiple future steps and demonstrates improved prediction accuracy over several baselines on four Chinese stock datasets.
methodology_description: The authors propose FDBRQ, a multistep stock price trend prediction pipeline that (1) transforms past adjusted closing price time series into frequency-domain embeddings using Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) followed by layer normalization, batch normalization, a set of full-dimension convolutions (kernel sizes 1..K), channel-average pooling and a fully-connected layer to produce per-time-step embeddings; (2) incorporates exogenous information via an external feature attention enhancement (EFAE) that computes an attention vector from selected external factors (softmax(W_A * F_T)) and applies elementwise weighting and residual addition to each embedding; (3) processes the enhanced embeddings through a bi-directional recurrent quantum network composed of two independent n-qubit chains of T Quantum Circuit Units (QCUs). Each QCU encodes the classical embedding into quantum state (quantum encoder) and evolves it with a parameterized quantum ansatz (trainable rotations and entangling gates) to produce a state phi_t which depends on phi_{t-1}; forward and backward circuit outputs are concatenated and projected by fully connected layers to produce per-step features, which are concatenated over time and mapped to q-step forecasts. Training is performed on classical hardware (quantum circuits are classically simulated as parameterized unitary layers) using the Adam optimizer (lr=0.001), a Huber-like loss (piecewise L2/L1), batch size 32, and 100 epochs. Input preprocessing includes adjusted-close filtering, removal of suspended trading dates, log-differencing (daily log-returns), min-max scaling; external factors are cleaned (forward-fill missing, MAD-based outlier clipping), neutralized for market cap and industry, standardized and selected via information coefficient (IC) and information ratio (IR). Experiments compare against ARIMA variants and several LSTM-based baselines on four CSI-300 constituent stocks over 1-, 5-, and 20-day horizons.
algorithms_used: Bi-directional recurrent quantum network (sequence of QCUs)
Baselines: ARIMA, WT-ARIMA, VMD-ARIMA, ARIMAX, LSTM, BLSTM, deep LSTM variants
dataset_used: Adjusted closing prices and factor data from JoinQuant for four CSI 300 constituent stocks (000651.XSHE, 300015.XSHE, 600519.XSHG, 601318.XSHG). Training period: 2018-01-01 to 2022-12-31; test period: 2023-01-01 to 2023-04-30 (78 trading days). External factors drawn from JoinQuant factor library (emotion, momentum, risk, style, technical factors).

preprocessing: Compute daily log-returns: x_t* = ln(x_t) - ln(x_{t-1})
Min–Max scaling of returns (then inverse-transform for outputs)
External factors: forward-fill missing values, MAD-based outlier clipping, market cap & industry neutralization, min–max standardization
Factor selection via Spearman IC and IR for 1D/5D/20D horizons; top factors per category chosen

pipeline_steps: For each prediction horizon set time-window length T (T=20 for 1-step, T=48 for 5-step, T=96 for 20-step).
Apply VMD to the T-length input series with K=7 modes to obtain K IMFs.
Arrange IMFs as feature map (K x T x 1), apply layer normalization then batch normalization.
Apply full-dimension convolutions with K kernels of receptive fields 1..K, then channel-average pooling to obtain 1 x K x T map.
Split along time axis into T feature vectors and map each via fully connected layer to embedding Et (demb=32).
Compute external attention At = softmax(W_A * F_T) from m external factors observed at last time T; produce enhanced embeddings Et' = At ⊗ Et ⊕ Et.
Feed enhanced embeddings sequentially into two independent n-qubit quantum circuits (forward and backward). Each circuit contains T Quantum Circuit Units (QCUs).

Each QCU: apply Quantum Encoder UE(Et') to encode classical features to qubit rotations, then apply parameterized Quantum Ansatz UA(theta_t) (depth dc=3) to evolve the state; initial state |0^n>. Use n=6 qubits.
At each timestep concatenate forward and backward quantum states and pass through fully connected layer to produce H_t (dh=32).
Concatenate H_t over time and apply final fully connected layer to output q-step predictions {y_t}_{t=1..q}.

Use Huber-like loss (piecewise L2 if |error|≥1 else |error|-0.5) and optimize trainable parameters (classical network weights and quantum ansatz parameters) with Adam (lr=0.001), batch size 32, epochs 100.

For baselines: ARIMA family models selected by AIC; WT-ARIMA and VMD-ARIMA use multiscale decomposition + per-component ARIMA and reconstruction; ARIMAX uses last-period covariates as constants for multistep rolling; LSTM variants configured with additional recurrent unit connected to external factors; deep models run 20 times and averaged.
training_notes: Model fine-tuned daily during testing by adding previous day to training set to simulate live updating
Quantum circuits are treated as parameterized unitary layers simulated on classical hardware; no specific quantum simulator or QPU is reported

experiment_output.predicted_outputs: q-step forecasts of closing price (multiplestep q=1,5,20) returned as time series of predicted prices (inverse-scaled and inverse-log-differenced back to price units).
experiment_output.result_format: Tabular metric comparisons per stock and horizon (RMSE, MAE, MAPE). Figures showing prediction traces with uncertainty bands (NNs run 20 times; light red band shows spread).

reproducibility_notes: Data: authors state that data used are available from the authors upon request; source is JoinQuant. Code and exact quantum-classical execution details (quantum simulator or framework, random seeds, initialization of ansatz parameters, measurement/shots if applicable, classical hardware specs) are not provided in the paper. The paper describes circuit structure (encoder + parameterized ansatz) and gate types (Rx/Ry/Rz/H, entangling operations) and hyperparameters (qubits=6, ansatz depth=3) which allow reimplementation, but lacking an accompanying codebase or simulator specification may hinder exact reproduction. Factor selection lists and preprocessing are described in sufficient detail to replicate factor inputs.
key_findings: [supported] The proposed FDBRQ (frequency-domain enhanced bi-directional recurrent quantum network) outperforms the compared baselines (ARIMA, WT-ARIMA, VMD-ARIMA, ARIMAX, LSTM, BLSTM, DLSTM, DBLSTM) on four Chinese-stock datasets for 1-, 5- and 20-step prediction tasks (tables 5–7).

[supported] The frequency-domain embedding module (FDEM) that uses VMD + normalization + convolution to produce time-step embeddings is causal (designed to avoid using future information) and was used in the experiments.

[supported] Incorporating external factors via the external feature attention enhancement (EFAE), where factors were selected by IC/IR analysis, improves predictive performance when included in the model.

[supported] Multistep prediction with neural-network-based models (including the proposed FDBRQ) reduces the error-accumulation problem seen in rolling-prediction ARIMA variants, yielding more stable multistep forecasts.

[supported] Practical constraints motivated using a small quantum system (6 qubits) in the implementation; the authors note that larger quantum neural networks are slow to train on classical hardware.
[speculative] The paper claims quantum neural networks have exponential memory capacity and eliminate catastrophic amnesia compared to classical networks.

[speculative] The authors claim that introducing quantum circuits into the neural network "improves the model’s understanding of the stock market" and that quantum parallelism enhances computational/adaptive capabilities.
[speculative] The assertion that information processing in the human brain is similar to quantum phenomena (citing quantum consciousness/quantum mind literature) is presented to motivate QNN use.

[speculative] The claim that the QCU-based bi-directional quantum network structure is the primary cause of the observed performance gains (i.e., that gains stem from quantum-specific properties rather than architecture/hyperparameter choices) is implied but not isolated experimentally.
results_summary: The authors introduce FDBRQ, combining a frequency-domain embedding (via VMD), an external-factor attention module (factors selected by IC/IR), and a bi-directional recurrent quantum neural network constructed from quantum circuit units (QCUs). On four CSI-300 constituent stocks and for 1-, 5-, and 20-step prediction horizons, FDBRQ attained the lowest reported RMSE/MAE/MAPE among the compared methods in the paper’s experiments. The paper highlights that multistep prediction with neural-network outputs avoids the cumulative error of rolling ARIMA-style forecasts, and attributes improved performance to the combined frequency-domain embedding, external-factor attention, and the quantum-circuit–based recurrent architecture. The authors also note practical limitations in scaling quantum-network size on classical hardware.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper attributes improved predictive performance to the inclusion of quantum circuit units and discusses theoretical quantum benefits (superposition, entanglement, quantum parallelism). However, experiments are run as model comparisons without demonstrating execution on quantum hardware, without isolating the quantum component's contribution (e.g., ablation vs. an equivalent classical architecture), and without provable/empirical quantum speedup or complexity advantage. Therefore any claimed 'quantum advantage' remains speculative.
limitations: When attempting to construct quantum neural networks with more qubits, training speed on classical computers becomes relatively slow (author-stated).
Building and operating large-scale quantum systems currently faces practical limitations in resources and cost, making large-qubit implementations challenging (author-stated).
The study evaluates the model on only four stocks from the Chinese market (CSI 300 constituents), which limits demonstrated generalizability to other assets, markets and market regimes [inferred].

The quantum circuits were evaluated in a classical computing environment (simulation) rather than on physical quantum hardware; therefore real-hardware noise, connectivity and runtime constraints are not assessed [inferred].

The model uses external factor values observed at the last period only; it does not model or require future exogenous covariates, which may limit scenarios where covariate evolution matters or where covariates can be forecasted explicitly [inferred].
Daily fine-tuning (adding the prior day to the training set) is used during testing, implying continual retraining and higher operational/computational cost in real-time deployment [inferred].

Selection of external factors was performed by IC/IR screening (top factors per category); this choice may miss other informative features and may be dataset-specific, impacting robustness [inferred].

Hyperparameter choices (e.g., T, K, n, dc, demb, dh) were fixed in experiments; sensitivity to these choices and hyperparameter optimization effects are not fully explored, limiting understanding of stability and reproducibility [inferred].

The contribution of the quantum components versus classical components (i.e., how much performance gain is attributable specifically to the quantum circuit design) is not isolated via detailed ablation on real quantum hardware, limiting causal attribution of improvements [inferred].
Interpretability of the learned quantum representations and decision rationale is not deeply examined; practical explainability for financial practitioners remains unclear [inferred].

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — The FDBRQ model (frequency-domain embedding + external feature attention + bi-directional recurrent quantum network) reports improved RMSE/MAE/MAPE versus ARIMA-family and multiple LSTM baselines on four CSI-300 constituent stocks across 1-, 5-, and 20-day horizons.

#idea:hybrid-approach — A classical preprocessing pipeline (VMD, normalization, convolutional feature extraction, attention-based factor integration) produces 32-d embeddings that are fed into parameterized quantum circuit units; training is performed classically with the quantum circuits simulated as parameterized unitary layers and optimized with Adam.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The temporal model uses two independent n-qubit chains (forward and backward) of T Quantum Circuit Units (QCUs); each QCU encodes the per-step embedding via a rotation-based quantum encoder and evolves it with a depth-3 parameterized ansatz, concatenating forward/backward states to produce timestep features.

#idea:hybrid-approach — External Feature Attention Enhancement (EFAE) integrates selected exogenous factors (selected by IC/IR) via a softmax weighting and residual addition to boost per-step embeddings prior to quantum processing.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum circuits were classically simulated as parameterized unitary layers; no experiments on physical QPUs or noisy-device simulators are reported.

#limitation:qubit-count — The implemented quantum recurrent network uses only n=6 qubits, indicating limited scale and potential difficulty extending to higher-dimensional inputs or production problems.

#limitation:data-encoding — Classical-to-quantum encoding is performed via qubit rotation encoders for 32-d embeddings, but the paper does not discuss state-preparation costs, circuit compilation overhead, or fidelity implications on real hardware.
